name: Oculomotor nerve (CN III)
func: Moves most of the eye muscles, letting the eye look up, down and inward, and lifts the upper eyelid. It also carries signals that shrink the pupil and focus the lens for near vision.

levels.kid:
The **oculomotor nerve** is a wire that runs from your brain to your eye. "Oculo" means eye and "motor" means move, so its name says it all: it **moves your eye**.

It pulls on little muscles so your eye can look **up**, look **down**, and look in toward your **nose**. It also lifts your **eyelid** so your eye can stay open.

And it has one more trick. When the sun is bright, this nerve makes the black circle in the middle of your eye, the **pupil**, get smaller, like closing a window shade so not too much light gets in.
levels.hs:
The **oculomotor nerve** is the third cranial nerve (**CN III**). It starts in the **midbrain**, from nuclei near the cerebral aqueduct at the level of the superior colliculus, and exits the front of the midbrain into the **interpeduncular fossa**. It then passes forward between the **posterior cerebral artery** and the **superior cerebellar artery**, runs alongside the **posterior communicating artery**, and travels through the wall of the **cavernous sinus** before entering the orbit through the **superior orbital fissure**.

It controls four of the six muscles that move the eye:
- **Superior rectus** (look up)
- **Inferior rectus** (look down)
- **Medial rectus** (look toward the nose)
- **Inferior oblique** (look up and out)

It also controls the **levator palpebrae superioris**, which lifts the upper eyelid.

Besides moving muscles, CN III carries **parasympathetic** fibers that constrict the **pupil** and change the shape of the **lens** to focus on near objects. When CN III is damaged, the eye drifts "**down and out**," the eyelid droops and the pupil may be wide.
levels.college:
The **oculomotor nuclear complex** has subnuclei for each muscle. Two quirks: the **superior rectus** subnucleus supplies the **opposite** eye (its fibers cross), and a single midline **central caudal nucleus** supplies **both** levator muscles. The **Edinger–Westphal nucleus** provides the preganglionic parasympathetic fibers.

In the cavernous sinus, CN III runs in the **lateral wall**, above CN IV, along with V1 and V2, while CN VI lies inside the sinus next to the internal carotid artery. Near the superior orbital fissure it divides into a **superior division** (superior rectus and levator) and an **inferior division** (medial rectus, inferior rectus, inferior oblique, plus the parasympathetic root to the **ciliary ganglion**). Both divisions pass through the **common tendinous ring** (annulus of Zinn).

Parasympathetic fibers synapse in the **ciliary ganglion**, which sits lateral to the optic nerve near the orbit's apex. Postganglionic **short ciliary nerves** supply the **sphincter pupillae** (miosis) and the **ciliary muscle** (accommodation).

The pupillary fibers run on the **outer (superficial) surface** of the nerve, mostly superomedially, which explains why compression and ischemia affect the pupil differently. The nerve is also tested in the **near triad**: convergence, accommodation and constriction.

Remember the eye muscle formula **LR6 SO4, the rest 3**: lateral rectus by CN VI, superior oblique by CN IV, everything else by CN III.
levels.phd:
CN III motor neurons belong to a special class: **extraocular motor neurons** fire at very high sustained rates (often over 100 spikes per second in fixation, with bursts far higher during saccades) and encode both eye position and velocity. They are relatively **resistant** to degeneration in **ALS**, a selective sparing linked to differences in calcium buffering (higher parvalbumin and calbindin), AMPA receptor composition and gene expression (for example IGF-2 and MMP-9 patterns).

Extraocular muscles themselves are distinct: they contain **multiply innervated fibers** with en grappe endings, alongside singly innervated twitch fibers, and express unique myosin isoforms. The **active pulley hypothesis** (Demer) proposes that connective tissue pulleys in the orbit shape muscle pulling directions, simplifying the neural control of eye movement (consistent with **Listing's law**).

Inputs: **saccade** commands arrive from the **riMLF** for vertical movements and via the **MLF** from abducens internuclear neurons for horizontal adduction. Vergence is driven by midbrain near-response cells near the oculomotor nucleus.

Development errors cause **congenital cranial dysinnervation disorders**. **CFEOM1** (mutations in **KIF21A**) leads to hypoplasia of the superior division of CN III, producing ptosis and restricted upgaze. **Duane syndrome** (often linked to **MAFB** or **CHN1**) involves an absent abducens nerve with aberrant innervation of the lateral rectus by CN III branches.

After injury, regrowing axons can be misrouted (**aberrant regeneration**), for example eyelid elevation on attempted downgaze (the pseudo-von Graefe sign). This happens after compressive lesions but typically not after microvascular ischemic palsies.
levels.expert:
A complete **CN III palsy** gives ptosis, an eye resting **down and out**, inability to adduct, elevate or depress, and a **fixed dilated pupil**.

The key clinical rule is about the **pupil**:
- **Pupil-involving** palsy suggests **compression** of the superficial pupillary fibers, classically a **posterior communicating artery aneurysm**. It is a neurosurgical emergency: urgent CTA or catheter angiography, then **clipping** or **endovascular coiling** before rupture causes a subarachnoid hemorrhage.
- **Pupil-sparing** palsy in an older patient with diabetes or hypertension is usually **microvascular ischemia** of the inner nerve core; it often recovers over weeks to months, though imaging is still commonly done.

In **uncal (transtentorial) herniation**, the medial temporal lobe compresses CN III against the tentorial edge, giving an ipsilateral **blown pupil**, often the first sign, before impaired consciousness and posturing. A unilateral dilated pupil in a head-injured patient demands urgent imaging and often decompression.

Other causes: midbrain stroke (**Weber** and **Benedikt** syndromes), **cavernous sinus** lesions (with IV, V1, V2 and VI involvement; e.g. carotid–cavernous fistula, thrombosis, tumor), **superior orbital fissure syndrome** and orbital apex syndrome (which also hits the optic nerve), **giant cell arteritis**, and **myasthenia gravis**, which can mimic a pupil-sparing palsy but never affects the pupil.

Imaging: **MRI with contrast** and **CTA/MRA** for aneurysm. Persistent double vision may be treated with prisms or strabismus surgery once stable.

keyPoints: CN III leaves the midbrain at the interpeduncular fossa, runs by the PComm artery and through the cavernous sinus wall
Supplies superior, inferior and medial recti, inferior oblique and the levator
Parasympathetic fibers (Edinger–Westphal → ciliary ganglion) constrict the pupil and focus the lens
Palsy: eye down and out, ptosis, ± dilated pupil
Pupil-involving palsy = think PComm aneurysm or uncal herniation

test.q: A complete CN III palsy leaves the eye resting:
test.explain: Unopposed lateral rectus (CN VI) and superior oblique (CN IV) pull the eye down and out.

test.q: A painful CN III palsy with a dilated pupil should make you worry most about a:
test.explain: Compression hits the superficial pupillary fibers first; this is a neurosurgical emergency.

test.q: Parasympathetic fibers of CN III synapse in the ______ ganglion.
test.explain: From the ciliary ganglion, short ciliary nerves supply the sphincter pupillae and ciliary muscle.

test.q: Which eye muscle is NOT supplied by CN III?
test.explain: LR6 SO4: the lateral rectus is CN VI, the superior oblique is CN IV.

test.q: The muscle that lifts the upper eyelid is the levator palpebrae ______.
test.explain: The levator is supplied by CN III, so a CN III palsy causes ptosis.
